title: Bitboard Attack Mask (Bit Manipulation)
real_world_story: A chess engine stores the whole board in a single 64-bit number so that move generation costs a few machine instructions instead of a double loop over squares. The engine needs the attack set of the queen, and any other piece standing in the way stops the queen's ray.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Board grid where '.' is an empty square and 'X' is a blocking piece
real_world_connection.query_represents: The square the queen stands on
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Setting one bit per square and OR-ing the eight rays until a blocker bit is hit

problem_statement: An engine stores the 8 x 8 board as a 64-bit bitboard, where bit (r * 8 + c) belongs to the square in row r and column c. Given the board of '.' (empty) and 'X' (a blocking piece) and the square (qr, qc) of a queen, count the squares the queen attacks. The queen moves any number of squares along its row, its column or either diagonal; the first blocking piece on a ray is attacked, and the ray stops there. The square the queen stands on is not counted.
task: Return the number of squares the queen attacks, counting the first blocker on each of the eight rays.
input_format: Eight lines each containing eight characters ('.' or 'X'). The final line contains two integers qr qc.
output_format: Print the number of attacked squares.
constraints: Board cells are empty (.) or a blocker (X)
The queen always stands on an empty square

examples.explanation: On an empty board a corner queen attacks 7 squares along its row, 7 along its column and 7 along its diagonal, which is 21 squares.

expected_algorithm.name: Bit Manipulation
expected_algorithm.reason: The whole board becomes one 64-bit integer, each ray walks with shifts, blockers are tested with AND, the attack set is built with OR and its size comes from a popcount.

complexity.time: O(1) because the board is a fixed 8 x 8 and only eight rays are walked

hint: Build one 64-bit mask with a 1 bit for every blocking square, using 1 shifted left by (row * 8 + col).
Walk each of the eight rays one square at a time, OR-ing the square's bit into the attack mask.
Stop a ray right after a square whose bit is set in the blocker mask, and count the bits at the end with popcount.
real_world_takeaway: Packing a board into a 64-bit bitboard turns attack generation into shifts, masks and popcount, which is why real engines generate moves so quickly.
